hints: Think what $E^{\circ}_{cell}$ measures, the voltage between two half cells, and what conditions must be fixed to make it standard.
walkthrough:
Picture what is being measured**
Imagine you connect any two half cells together and read the voltage. That reading is the cell potential. To make it standard, you fix everything that could change the voltage, so concentration, temperature and pressure are all at their standard values.
Final answer: The e.m.f. of a cell formed by two half cells under standard conditions ($1.0 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ solutions, $298 \, \text{K}$, $1 \, \text{atm}$ for gases).

hints: Look at the two separate beakers in the diagram and think how you complete the electrical circuit without mixing the two solutions.
walkthrough:
Complete the circuit in two places**
You already have two half cells but they are isolated. Electrons need a path through the outer wires, so join the two metal electrodes through a voltmeter which reads $E_{cell}$ without drawing current. Ions need a path between the solutions to balance charge, so dip a salt bridge containing an inert electrolyte between the two beakers.
Final answer: Connect the two electrodes with a (high resistance) voltmeter via wires and connect the two solutions with a salt bridge.

hints: Recall the difference between a metal dipping in its own ions and a half cell where both species are ions in solution.
Think which half cell, $\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}$ or $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$, needs a solid metal of its own and which needs an inert carrier for electrons.
Remember that for the ion only system both oxidation states must be present together in the same solution at $1.0 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Sort the metal ion system**
$\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}$ has a solid metal available. So the electrode A is simply silver metal dipping into a solution B containing its own ions, $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})$. Under standard conditions that is $1.0 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Ag}^{+}$.

Sort the ion ion system**
$\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ has no solid Fe electrode involved, both species are aqueous ions. Electrons cannot flow in and out through solution alone, so you need an inert metal to conduct electrons without reacting. That is platinum, so C is $\text{Pt}$.

Place both ions together**
Because the platinum is inert, the solution around it must contain both halves of the redox couple. So D is a mixture of $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$, both at $1.0 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ for standard conditions.

Final answer: A = $\text{Ag}$ (silver electrode)
B = $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})$, e.g. $1.0 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{AgNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$
C = $\text{Pt}$ (platinum electrode)
D = $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$, both $1.0 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ (A/B and C/D may be reversed).

hints: Compare $E^{\circ}(\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}) = +0.80 \, \text{V}$ with $E^{\circ}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77 \, \text{V}$ and decide which species is the stronger oxidant.
walkthrough:
Let the more positive half cell win**
The Data Booklet gives $E^{\circ} = +0.80 \, \text{V}$ for $\text{Ag}^{+}+\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}$ and $+0.77 \, \text{V}$ for $\text{Fe}^{3+}+\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}^{2+}$. The more positive value is reduced, so $\text{Ag}^{+}$ takes electrons while $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is oxidised to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. Combine the two half equations, cancelling $\text{e}^{-}$, to give $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \longrightarrow \text{Ag}(\text{s}) + \text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$.

hints: Start with $E = E^{\circ} + 0.059 \log[\text{Ag}^{+}]$ and think whether lowering $[\text{Ag}^{+}]$ below $1.0 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ will lower or raise $E$.
After finding the new $E$ for the silver electrode, subtract the unchanged $E(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+})$ to get $E_{cell}$.
walkthrough:
Apply Nernst to the changed electrode**
Only $[\text{Ag}^{+}]$ changes, so only the silver potential changes. Substitute directly:
$$E = E^{\circ} + 0.059 \log[\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})]$$
$$E = 0.80 + 0.059 \log(0.31)$$
Since $\log(0.31) = -0.51$, the correction is $0.059 \times (-0.51) = -0.030 \, \text{V}$. That makes sense, lower reactant ion concentration makes reduction less favourable, so $E$ falls to about $0.77 \, \text{V}$.

Recombine to get the cell e.m.f.**
The iron half cell is still standard at $+0.77 \, \text{V}$. So:
$$E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode} = 0.77 - 0.77 = 0.00 \, \text{V}$$
The two electrode potentials are now equal, so there is no driving force and the measured $E_{cell}$ is $0.0 \, \text{V}$.
